title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
hookLine: the second telling: God shapes a human from the dust and breathes into its nose

lines: FROM HIGH ABOVE, THEN THE GROUND.
cards: Turn one page in Genesis and the story starts again. Chapter one told it from high above: days, lights, a world spoken into order, people made last. Chapter two drops down to the ground.
No rain yet, no one to work the soil, just a mist coming up from the earth and watering it. And instead of speaking from a distance, God gets close. Hands in the dirt.
The first chapter was a cathedral. The second is a workshop.

teach.h: FORMED, LIKE A POTTER WITH CLAY.
teach.b: Here's the verse in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."
Formed: the Hebrew verb is the one used for a potter shaping clay. Then a pun English loses. The ground is adamah.
The human made from it is adam. Earthling from the earth. Adam isn't first a name here; it's a word for a human being, a creature of soil.
Then the breath. God doesn't speak this one into being.
God leans in and breathes into its nose, and the clay becomes a living soul, in Hebrew a nefesh, a living being. This telling differs from chapter one.
The order changes, and even the name for God changes: chapter one says God, chapter two says the LORD God, the personal name.
Many scholars think two older accounts were set side by side. Many Christians read them as two views of one event, a wide shot and a close-up. Either way, the book kept both.
And the close-up says something about a person. You are dust, made of the same stuff as the ground under your shoes.

teach.h: AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.
teach.b: And you are breath, given by God from close up. Not one or the other. In churches that keep Ash Wednesday, the ashes often go on with words from the next chapter: dust thou art.
And many Christians link the breath with the Spirit; in both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit can also mean breath.

how: On Ash Wednesday many Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist Christians receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often with words drawn from Genesis 3:19 about returning to dust.

o: the breath of life God gives a person
the ground, the soil a human is shaped from
the first man's personal name in Hebrew

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: in Genesis 2, Adam is first of all a personal name
adam is a word for a human, a creature from the adamah, the ground.
Genesis 2 tells creation again, in a different order
chapter one tells it from high above; chapter two starts again, close up, on the ground.
the name used for God changes between chapters one and two
chapter one says God; chapter two says the LORD God, the personal name.

games.q: God has shaped a human from the dust of the ground. it's lying there, clay. what does God do next?
o: speaks a word from far away.
leans in and breathes into its nose.
leaves it to dry in the sun.
games.why: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." chapter one spoke from above. here God comes close.

practice: Feel your weight, your feet on the floor, your body heavy in the chair: that's the dust. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, five times, slower each time, and notice the air coming in: that's the breath.
If you pray, you can give thanks for the breath you didn't have to make.

wordCard.voice: Adamah. The Hebrew word for ground, the soil a human, adam, was shaped from, then given breath to live.

orig.note: Hebrew: ground, soil. The human made from it is adam, an earthling from the earth.

carryVoice: Your line: dust with breath in it. Both halves, every day. Day three hundred thirty-five.
